clue.text: Retrospective skill with which some politicians identify Mark Twain and W. H. Davies

definitions.text: Mark Twain and W. H. Davies

indicators.note: looking back, so the word for skill is read from its end to its start

parts.note: art is skill or craft
MPs are Members of Parliament, some politicians

explanation.surface: A backward-looking talent that politicians share with two famous wandering writers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retrospective' looks like a description of the skill but signals the turnaround. Twain wrote A Tramp Abroad and Davies The Autobiography of a Super-Tramp.
explanation.definitionFit: Both authors wrote of themselves as vagrant wanderers, Twain abroad and Davies as a super-tramp.

clue.text: Captain Dorling's river bird

definitions.note: Henry Taprell Dorling wrote naval stories under the pen name Captain Taffrail

parts.note: the Taff is a river in South Wales
a rail is a marsh bird

explanation.surface: A naval captain owns a stretch of riverbed.
explanation.walkthrough: The page as held reads 'bed', but the wordplay needs the bird RAIL. Dorling's pen name is also the rail round a ship's stern.
explanation.definitionFit: It was the pseudonym under which the naval officer Dorling published his sea stories.

clue.text: In his panic, he saw life as a used car dump

definitions.text: In his panic, he saw life as a used car dump

parts.words: In his panic, he saw life as a used car dump
parts.note: a Spanish playwright who founded the Panic movement and wrote The Car Cemetery, set among wrecked vehicles

explanation.surface: A frightened man sees his life as a scrapyard of old cars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Panic' is the Panic Movement he co-founded, not fear; his play El cementerio de automóviles is set in a car dump.
explanation.definitionFit: The playwright co-founded the Panic Movement and wrote a play set in a car cemetery.

clue.text: An hour in relief column for Jacobean dramatic hero

indicators.note: the hour's letter sits inside the column word

parts.note: a pilaster is a flat column projecting in relief from a wall
H is the abbreviation for hour

explanation.surface: Sixty minutes spent inside a sculpted column for an old stage hero.
explanation.walkthrough: Beaumont and Fletcher's play Philaster, or Love Lies a-Bleeding, is named after its hero.
explanation.definitionFit: The title hero of a Beaumont and Fletcher tragicomedy from the Jacobean stage.

clue.text: Reade brought it closer, oddly enough, to home

definitions.text: Reade brought it closer, oddly enough, to home

indicators.note: signals that the letters of the two words are strangely reordered

explanation.surface: A novelist brought something nearer to the house, strangely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly enough' rearranges IT and CLOSER. Charles Reade's novel The Cloister and the Hearth pairs this word with the hearth, which is home.
explanation.definitionFit: Reade's novel title links a monastic enclosure with the hearth, a byword for home.

clue.text: She of The Lake?

parts.note: a titled woman named after an English Lake District lake, heroine of Wilde's play about a fan

explanation.surface: A question about the Arthurian Lady of the Lake.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lady of the Lake suggests Arthurian legend, but Windermere is England's largest lake and Wilde's heroine bears its name.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilde's heroine is a titled woman whose name is that of a Cumbrian lake.

clue.text: Hammond gets directions to pub

parts.note: an inn is a pub
E and S are compass points, east and south

explanation.surface: Someone called Hammond is told the way to the local.
explanation.walkthrough: Hammond is the forename of the thriller writer Hammond Innes, not the surname it looks like.
explanation.definitionFit: The thriller novelist wrote under the name Hammond, so the forename identifies his surname.

clue.text: Some great actor, mentally in anguish

indicators.note: only part of the run of words is used, the letters lying across actor and mentally

explanation.surface: A distinguished performer suffers inner torment.
explanation.definitionFit: Torment and anguish are both severe mental suffering.

clue.text: Regretting introduction of Raven's Unman, even in new guise

indicators.note: the opening letter of each following word is taken

explanation.surface: Simon Raven's play Unman, Wittering and Zigo is staged again in a new form.
explanation.walkthrough: Unman, Wittering and Zigo is a play by Giles Cooper, though the surface credits Raven, a novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: To rue is to feel sorry for, so its present participle means feeling regret.

clue.text: "One of our gentlemen found time to say *How delicious!" before he died", she said

definitions.text: "One of our gentlemen found time to say *How delicious!" before he died", she said

parts.words: "One of our gentlemen found time to say *How delicious!" before he died", she said
parts.note: a line spoken by one of the poisoning spinster aunts in Arsenic and Old Lace about their elderberry wine

explanation.surface: A woman recalls a gentleman's dying compliment on something he tasted.
explanation.walkthrough: In Kesselring's Arsenic and Old Lace the two sweet old aunts poison lonely gentlemen with elderberry wine.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the murderous elderly sisters in Arsenic and Old Lace speaks this line.

clue.text: Werewolf defined by Webster

parts.note: the duke in The Duchess of Malfi by John Webster goes mad with lycanthropy

explanation.surface: A dictionary entry for a werewolf.
explanation.walkthrough: Webster suggests the dictionary, but it is the playwright John Webster, whose Duke of Calabria believes he is a wolf.
explanation.definitionFit: The Duchess of Malfi's brother, the duke, suffers lycanthropy in Webster's tragedy.

clue.text: Scandinavian part of minor Seneca tragedy

indicators.note: the letters are a piece taken out of the words minor and Seneca run together

explanation.surface: A Nordic element found in a lesser tragedy by Seneca.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Norse is the Scandinavian language and people of the Vikings.

clue.text: Scott's Sir Hugh steals paintings, apparently

parts.note: robs means steals
art means paintings collectively

explanation.surface: A Scott character is caught pilfering pictures.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Hugh Robsart is the father of Amy Robsart in Scott's Kenilworth.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Hugh is Amy's father in Kenilworth, sharing her family name.

clue.text: Light reading for Fielding squire

definitions.meaning: Squire ..., Sophia's boisterous father in Tom Jones

explanation.surface: Easy fiction for a country gentleman from a Fielding novel.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowboy novel is undemanding reading; Fielding's Tom Jones has the hunting Squire Western.

clue.text: Innisfree, for example, is rented out?

parts.note: let means rented out

explanation.surface: Is Yeats's island retreat being leased?
explanation.walkthrough: Yeats's poem The Lake Isle of Innisfree names a tiny island in Lough Gill.
explanation.definitionFit: Innisfree is a small island, the subject of Yeats's famous poem.

clue.text: Supply critical comment for the year of the Gallery?

parts.note: anno is Latin for in the year
the Tate is the London art gallery

explanation.surface: Writing a critique of the Gallery's year.
explanation.definitionFit: To add explanatory or critical notes to a text.

clue.text: Sassoon said that soldiers draw no dividend from those of time

definitions.text: Sassoon said that soldiers draw no dividend from those of time

parts.words: Sassoon said that soldiers draw no dividend from those of time
parts.note: a line from Siegfried Sassoon's war poem Dreamers about soldiers having no future days

explanation.surface: A quotation from a war poet about soldiers' prospects.
explanation.walkthrough: Sassoon's Dreamers says soldiers 'draw no dividend from time's to-morrows'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sassoon's soldiers have no future days to gain from, as they may die.

clue.text: The end of Joseph Johnson's review

definitions.text: The end of Joseph Johnson's review

parts.words: The end of Joseph Johnson's review
parts.note: the publisher Joseph Johnson ran the Analytical Review; the close examination such a review offers is its aim

explanation.surface: The final part of a review published by Joseph Johnson.
explanation.walkthrough: Joseph Johnson, not Samuel, published the Analytical Review, whose purpose was careful critical scrutiny.
explanation.definitionFit: Detailed examination is the purpose of a critical review like Johnson's Analytical Review.

clue.text: Game-bird habitat in holiday rhyme

parts.note: the partridge's perch in the carol The Twelve Days of Christmas

explanation.surface: Where a game bird lives in a Christmas song.
explanation.definitionFit: The carol's first gift is a partridge sitting in a fruit tree.

clue.text: Germaine Greer thought they could be female

definitions.text: Germaine Greer thought they could be female

parts.words: Germaine Greer thought they could be female
parts.note: a reference to Greer's feminist book The Female Eunuch

explanation.surface: A feminist's view of who might be a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Greer's 1970 book The Female Eunuch argued women were cut off from their own power.
explanation.definitionFit: Greer's book title pairs the word female with castrated men.

clue.text: Mother and Child by The Master Builder

parts.note: ma is mother
a son is a child

explanation.surface: A painting of Mother and Child attributed to Ibsen's play.
explanation.walkthrough: The Master Builder suggests Ibsen's play, but here it is simply a skilled builder in stone.
explanation.definitionFit: A mason is a craftsman who builds in stone.

clue.text: Poet's ballad knight and queen

definitions.note: the 's stands for is, joining the definition to the wordplay

parts.note: Sir Patrick Spens is the hero of the Scottish ballad
ER, Elizabeth Regina, means queen

explanation.surface: A poet's ballad about a knight and a queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Patrick Spens is a Scottish ballad of a knight sent to sea by his king.
explanation.definitionFit: Edmund Spenser was the Elizabethan poet of The Faerie Queene.

clue.text: It was unexpectedly sprung by Hopkins

definitions.text: It was unexpectedly sprung by Hopkins

parts.words: It was unexpectedly sprung by Hopkins
parts.note: Gerard Manley Hopkins invented the metre called sprung ...

explanation.surface: Someone called Hopkins sprang a surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sprung' suggests a surprise, but Hopkins's sprung rhythm counts stresses rather than syllables.
explanation.definitionFit: Hopkins's metrical system is known as sprung rhythm, a pattern of beats.

clue.text: Hamlet needed a south wind properly to identify one

definitions.text: Hamlet needed a south wind properly to identify one

parts.words: Hamlet needed a south wind properly to identify one
parts.note: Hamlet says that when the wind is southerly he knows a hawk from this tool

explanation.surface: Hamlet's claim that he can tell things apart in a southerly wind.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet: 'I am but mad north-north-west: when the wind is southerly I know a hawk from a handsaw.'
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet contrasts a hawk with a carpenter's saw to show he is sane.

clue.text: Ironic comment heard from woodland god

indicators.note: the word for ironic comment is spoken, giving a word of similar sound

parts.note: satire is ironic or mocking comment

explanation.surface: A mocking remark is overheard from a forest deity.
explanation.definitionFit: Satyrs are half-goat woodland spirits of Greek myth.

clue.text: Wonder absorbs student poet

indicators.note: the word for wonder takes in another letter

parts.note: a marvel is a wonder
L, a learner, means student

explanation.surface: A marvel takes in a young student poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Andrew Marvell was the 17th-century metaphysical poet.

clue.text: Roman orator loses American connection, that's understood ()

indicators.note: the Roman's name drops some letters

parts.note: Tacitus was a Roman orator and historian
US is the United States, the American link

explanation.surface: A Roman speaker loses his link with America, it is implied.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacit means implied or understood without being said.

clue.text: One of Lawrence's slower-moving publications

parts.note: D. H. Lawrence's 1921 sequence of poems about slow reptiles

explanation.surface: A poorly selling book by Lawrence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slower-moving' suggests poor sales, but Lawrence's poem sequence is about slow shelled reptiles.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawrence published a poem cycle named after slow-moving shelled reptiles.

clue.text: Rimes all wrong before psalm

indicators.note: the letters of rimes are put wrongly, in a new order

parts.note: ere is an old word for before

explanation.surface: Badly rhymed lines precede a psalm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all wrong' turns RIMES into MISER.
explanation.definitionFit: Psalm 51 in Latin begins with this word, and settings of it are sung.

clue.text: Very big flower for god

parts.note: OS is outsize, very big
an iris is a flower

explanation.surface: A huge flower for a deity.
explanation.definitionFit: Osiris is the Egyptian deity of the dead.
